extracted.intended_audience: fiction writers preparing a one-page synopsis for agents or query packages (e.g., Pitch Wars applicants)
extracted.subtask_description: Instructions and criteria for drafting and trimming a one-page, single-spaced synopsis of a novel for literary agents and submission packages. Covers what to include, how to structure, and practical editing/trimming techniques so the synopsis fits one page while conveying the full plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish synopsis from summary
rubrics_metrics.description: A synopsis is not a summary; a synopsis is like the Cliff’s Notes version of your book and should include spoilers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When you hear “summary,” think teaser copy (query letter or jacket copy). A synopsis must give a brief recap of all that happens in your manuscript—'Divulge, divulge, divulge.' This is not the time to leave the reader hanging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tell the full plot from beginning to end
rubrics_metrics.description: Begin by thoroughly writing out your plot — tell the story of your novel from beginning to end as clearly as you can recall it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't economize language in the first draft; be thorough now because you'll shorten later. Make sure the synopsis covers the arc up through resolution/denouement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use chapter notes or a style sheet to build the draft
rubrics_metrics.description: Skim through your book and take notes on the happenings in each chapter to support a thorough initial synopsis draft.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you have a copyeditor, request a style sheet with chapter synopses to shortcut this step. Recounting plot from memory is possible but less reliable than chapter notes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Take a break between drafting and editing
rubrics_metrics.description: After drafting the full-plot synopsis, step away before you start trimming so your brain shifts from generation to editing mode.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The break helps you be more objective during the fiddly trimming process; it may take more than one sitting to finish.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trim ruthlessly to one single-spaced page
rubrics_metrics.description: Scale back your lengthy synopsis to a single-spaced page — this is often the hardest part of the process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on economy of language and structural cuts rather than trying to rewrite elegantly at first. The target is a compact, complete narrative on one page.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure sentence-level relevance to plot
rubrics_metrics.description: Read through and ask if each sentence is relevant to the plot; remove sentences that aren’t clearly necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For books with many subplots, prioritize the primary story arc. If a sentence or phrase is a 'maybe', cut it out. Being non-precious is critical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omit or de-emphasize subplots when necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: When space is limited, stick to the primary story arc and drop secondary subplots that don't serve the central narrative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a practical editorial choice rather than a value judgment about those subplots; the agent wants the main through-line on one page.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cut unnecessary adjectives and adverbs
rubrics_metrics.description: Reduce descriptive modifiers to keep language economical and allow space for plot beats.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A pass specifically for adjectives/adverbs helps tighten prose; favor verbs and concrete nouns that carry meaning without ornament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use structural frameworks (Freytag’s pyramid / three-act) to balance coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Use Freytag’s pyramid or the three-act structure as a metric to judge whether your synopsis is allocating page space appropriately across exposition, rising action, climax, falling action, and denouement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look at the page in approximate fifths: if exposition takes up three-fifths, trim it and move on. The framework helps ensure you reach and describe the climax and resolution succinctly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Line- and paragraph-level trimming to fit page
rubrics_metrics.description: When you're nearly at one page, examine paragraphs that end near the start of a new line to pare back sentences and gain space.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small edits in these paragraphs are more likely to move the whole synopsis up one line than lengthy rewrites elsewhere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Get targeted feedback from someone who's read the manuscript
rubrics_metrics.description: Share your near-final one-page synopsis with a writing friend who has read your full manuscript to identify removable phrases or unclear beats.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A reader familiar with the book can spot redundancies or missing essentials and suggest cuts that preserve clarity while saving space.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrate alignment between synopsis and manuscript
rubrics_metrics.description: Make sure the synopsis accurately reflects what the novel actually delivers, since agents will use it to judge how well long-form writing aligns with the synopsis’s promises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inconsistencies between synopsis and manuscript can signal the need for revision or that the project may require extra editorial hand-holding; be truthful and clear about tone, stakes, and major plot outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt the right mindset: be concise and persistent
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that trimming to one page is a soft skill like elevator pitching and may take multiple sessions; don't be disheartened.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Persist through fiddly edits, and remember the purpose: a succinct, complete pitch that benefits many publishing scenarios (agents, contests, pitches).
